titulo_es: Past modals: shades of meaning (needn't have, should have, would have)
descripcion_es: needn't have vs didn't need to; should have, could have, might have, must have, can't have, would have.
resumen: Modal + have + past participle expresses deductions, criticism, unrealised possibilities or hypotheses about the past. Some pairs have shades of meaning that Spanish does not distinguish, such as needn't have done versus didn't need to do.

filas: The ground is wet; it must have rained.
She can't have finished already; she only started at ten.
He might have missed the bus.
You should have told me earlier.
Something that was done and was not a good idea
I shouldn't have eaten so much.
We could have won if we'd tried harder.
I would have helped you, but nobody asked me.
It was done, but it wasn't necessary
You needn't have brought wine; we had plenty.
It wasn't necessary (usually it wasn't done)
I didn't need to wake up early, so I slept in.

explicacion.texto: Needn't have done always implies that the action WAS carried out and turned out to be unnecessary. Didn't need to do only indicates that it was not necessary; the normal interpretation is that it was not done, although the context can make the opposite clear (I didn't need to go, but I went anyway).

items: Must have has no meaning of obligation in the past: for that you use had to (I had to work late).
The negative deduction is can't have or couldn't have, not mustn't have.
Could have can express possibility (It could have been him) or an ability that was not used (You could have called me).
Was/were supposed to have done = they were expected to have done it (and they didn't).

ejemplos.frase: You needn't have waited for me; I had my keys.
ejemplos.traduccion: No hacía falta que me esperaras; tenía mis llaves.

ejemplos.frase: The shop was empty, so we didn't need to queue.
ejemplos.traduccion: La tienda estaba vacía, así que no tuvimos que hacer cola.

ejemplos.frase: She must have forgotten our appointment.
ejemplos.traduccion: Se le debe de haber olvidado nuestra cita.

ejemplos.frase: He can't have written this; he doesn't speak German.
ejemplos.traduccion: No puede haberlo escrito él; no habla alemán.

ejemplos.frase: We should have booked a table in advance.
ejemplos.traduccion: Deberíamos haber reservado mesa con antelación.

ejemplos.frase: I would have called you, but my phone was dead.
ejemplos.traduccion: Te habría llamado, pero me quedé sin batería.

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: For negative deduction in the past you use can't/couldn't have; mustn't expresses prohibition.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I must have studied yesterday, so I couldn't go out.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I had to study yesterday, so I couldn't go out.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Past obligation is had to; must have is deduction (Spanish “debe de haber”).
Modal + have + past participle; have cannot be left out.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: You didn't need to bring a cake, but thank you!
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: You needn't have brought a cake, but thank you!
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: If the action was done and turned out to be unnecessary, the natural choice is needn't have + past participle.

ejercicios.frase: I ___ so much food; only three people came to the party.
respuestas: needn't have bought
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule in the table applies: “needn't have done: it was done, but it wasn't necessary”, with the clarification that needn't have always implies that the action was carried out. The clue is the second part, “only three people came”: the food had already been bought and it turned out to be too much. So the form is needn't + have + bought, the past participle of buy. None of the other options expresses an action that was done and was unnecessary.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Food was bought and it turned out to be unnecessary: needn't have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: No hacía falta que comprara tanta comida; solo vinieron tres personas a la fiesta.

por_opcion.can't have bought: Incorrect. Can't have expresses a negative deduction (“it can't be that I bought”); it makes no sense to make a deduction about your own purchase.
por_opcion.needn't have bought: Correct. Needn't have + past participle indicates that the purchase was made and turned out to be unnecessary.
por_opcion.mustn't have bought: Incorrect. Mustn't expresses prohibition and is not used for deductions about the past; the negative deduction is can't have.
por_opcion.couldn't buy: Incorrect. Couldn't buy means “I wasn't able to buy”, which contradicts the idea of having bought too much.

ejercicios.frase: It was a holiday, so I ___ go to work. I stayed in bed.
respuestas: didn't need to
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “didn't need to do: it wasn't necessary (usually it wasn't done)” applies. The clue is “I stayed in bed”: the action was not carried out, so you cannot use needn't have, which requires that it was done. Also, the gap is followed by the infinitive go, and didn't need to is the only option that is built with to + infinitive. The result is “I didn't need to go to work”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: It wasn't necessary and it wasn't done: didn't need to + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: Era festivo, así que no tenía que ir a trabajar. Me quedé en la cama.

por_opcion.needn't have: Incorrect. Needn't have requires a past participle (gone) and means that the action was done; here the person didn't go to work.
por_opcion.didn't need to: Correct. Didn't need to + infinitive indicates that it wasn't necessary, and the context confirms that it wasn't done.
por_opcion.shouldn't have: Incorrect. Shouldn't have expresses criticism of something that was done, and it would also need a past participle, not go.
por_opcion.can't have: Incorrect. Can't have is a negative deduction about the past and it also requires a past participle.

ejercicios.frase: The lights are off. They ___ gone to bed.
respuestas: must have
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “must have done: almost certain deduction (Spanish “debe de haber…”)” applies. The clue is the evidence in the first sentence, “The lights are off”, which leads to a logical conclusion about the past. The form is must + have + gone, with the past participle of go already given in the sentence. Should have would be criticism, not a deduction.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Almost certain deduction from evidence: must have.
ejercicios.traduccion: Las luces están apagadas. Deben de haberse ido a la cama.

por_opcion.must have: Correct. Must have + past participle expresses an almost certain deduction from evidence.
por_opcion.should have: Incorrect. Should have expresses criticism or what would have been advisable (“they ought to have left”), not a deduction.
por_opcion.needn't have: Incorrect. Needn't have indicates something done unnecessarily; it makes no sense here.
por_opcion.can't have: Incorrect. Can't have expresses impossibility, the opposite of what the lights being off suggests.

ejercicios.frase: She ___ stolen the money; she was abroad at the time.
respuestas: can't have
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “can't / couldn't have done: negative deduction” applies, together with the key point that the negative deduction is can't have or couldn't have, not mustn't have. The clue is the alibi “she was abroad at the time”, which makes the theft impossible. The result is can't + have + stolen. Mustn't have is the most frequent calque of Spanish “no debe de haber”, but in English mustn't expresses prohibition.
ejercicios.traduccion: No puede haber robado el dinero; estaba en el extranjero en ese momento.

por_opcion.mustn't have: Incorrect. Mustn't expresses prohibition; for negative deduction in the past you use can't have or couldn't have.
por_opcion.can't have: Correct. Can't have + past participle expresses that something is impossible in the light of evidence.
por_opcion.shouldn't have: Incorrect. Shouldn't have criticises something that was actually done (“she shouldn't have stolen it”), which contradicts the alibi.
por_opcion.needn't have: Incorrect. Needn't have indicates that something unnecessary was done; it does not express impossibility.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the correct form.
ejercicios.frase: You look exhausted. You should ___ (go) to bed earlier last night.
respuestas: have gone
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “should / ought to have done: criticism or regret (Spanish “debería haber…”)” applies. The clue is “last night”: something in the past that was not done is being criticised, and the modal should is already in the sentence. After the modal you need have plus the past participle of go, which is gone. The result is “You should have gone to bed earlier”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Criticism about the past: should have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Pareces agotado. Deberías haberte acostado antes anoche.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Have is missing: the structure is modal + have + past participle, and have cannot be left out.
Went is the past simple; after have you need the past participle gone.
Should go would refer to the present or the future; to criticise the past you need should have gone.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the correct form.
ejercicios.frase: I don't know where Tom is. He might ___ (miss) the train this morning.
respuestas: have missed
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “may / might / could have done: possibility about the past” applies. The clue is “I don't know where Tom is” and “this morning”: the speaker speculates about a past cause without certainty. After might you need have and the regular past participle missed. The result is “He might have missed the train”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Possibility about the past: might have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: No sé dónde está Tom. Puede que haya perdido el tren esta mañana.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Have is missing: might missed is not possible; the modal is followed by have + past participle.
Might miss would refer to a future possibility; for the past you need might have missed.
After a modal, have is not conjugated: it is always have, never has.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the correct form.
ejercicios.frase: If you had asked, I would ___ (lend) you my car.
respuestas: have lent
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “would have done: hypothetical result, willingness” applies. The clue is the unreal past condition “If you had asked”, which requires would have + past participle in the main clause (third conditional). The past participle of lend is irregular: lent. The result is “I would have lent you my car”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Hypothetical result in the past: would have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si me lo hubieras pedido, te habría prestado el coche.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Lend is irregular and its past participle is lent, not lend.
Lend is not regular: the past participle is lent, not lended.
Would lend is the second conditional (present or future); with “If you had asked” you need would have lent.

ejercicios.frase: Yesterday I ___ to finish the report before five, so I couldn't leave early.
respuestas: had
ejercicios.explicacion: The key point in this unit applies: “Must have has no meaning of obligation in the past: for that you use had to”. The clue is “Yesterday” and the consequence “so I couldn't leave early”: this is about a real obligation that was fulfilled. Before to finish only had fits, the past of have to. The result is “I had to finish the report”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Obligation in the past is expressed with had to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ayer tuve que terminar el informe antes de las cinco, así que no pude salir pronto.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Must has no past form and must to does not exist; past obligation is had to.
Needed to would be correct in another context, but the obligation this unit practises here is had to.
Should does not take to and expresses advice, not an obligation fulfilled in the past.

ejercicios.frase: He mustn't have heard the alarm; he slept through it.
respuestas: He can't have heard the alarm; he slept through it.
He couldn't have heard the alarm; he slept through it.
He cannot have heard the alarm; he slept through it.
ejercicios.explicacion: The key point applies: “The negative deduction is can't have or couldn't have, not mustn't have”. The clue is “he slept through it”: the fact that he kept sleeping shows that it is impossible that he heard the alarm. The correction is “He can't have heard” (or couldn't have, cannot have). Mustn't expresses prohibition and cannot be used for deduction.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Negative deduction in the past: can't/couldn't have.
ejercicios.traduccion: No puede haber oído la alarma; siguió durmiendo sin enterarse.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He mustn't have heard the alarm; he slept through it.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: mustn't does not express negative deduction, but prohibition.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He must not have heard the alarm; he slept through it.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without the contraction it is still the same problem; in American usage you hear must not have, but this unit and the British norm require can't have.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He can't hear the alarm; he slept through it.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Can't hear refers to the present; to make a deduction about the past you need can't have heard.

glosario.significado: seguir durmiendo sin enterarse de algo

ejercicios.frase: You could warned me about the traffic.
respuestas: You could have warned me about the traffic.
ejercicios.explicacion: The general rule “modal + have + past participle” applies, together with the key point that could have can express an ability or opportunity not taken. The clue is the implicit reproach: the speaker complains that nobody warned them. The mistake is leaving out have; the correction is “You could have warned me”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: You could warned me about the traffic.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: have is missing between could and the past participle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: You could warn me about the traffic.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Could warn refers to the present (“you could warn me”); for a reproach about the past you need could have warned.

errores_previstos.respuesta: You could have warn me about the traffic.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After have you need the past participle warned, not the infinitive.

ejercicios.frase: It wasn't necessary for you to clean the kitchen, but you did.
respuestas: You needn't have cleaned the kitchen.
You needn't have cleaned the kitchen, but you did.
You need not have cleaned the kitchen.
You need not have cleaned the kitchen, but you did.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule applies that needn't have done always implies that the action was carried out and turned out to be unnecessary. The clue is “but you did”: the kitchen was cleaned. So the form is needn't + have + cleaned, and the tag but you did can be kept or left out, because needn't have already implies it. The uncontracted form need not have is also acceptable.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Action done but unnecessary: needn't have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: No hacía falta que limpiaras la cocina (pero la limpiaste).

errores_previstos.respuesta: You didn't need to clean the kitchen.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Didn't need to is usually understood as meaning that it wasn't done; besides, the instruction asks for needn't have.

errores_previstos.respuesta: You needn't have clean the kitchen.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After have you need the past participle cleaned, not the infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: You needn't to have cleaned the kitchen.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Needn't works as a modal and does not take to.

respuestas: She must have left early.
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “must have done: almost certain deduction” applies. The original sentence, “I'm sure she left early”, expresses certainty about the past, which is exactly the meaning of must have. The past simple left becomes have + past participle, which is also left. The result is “She must have left early”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Certainty about the past: must have + past participle.

errores_previstos.explicacion: After have you need the past participle left, not the infinitive.
Have is missing: modal + have + past participle.
Had to expresses obligation (“she was obliged to leave”), not the deduction that “I'm sure” requires.

ejercicios.frase: It was a mistake to tell him the secret.
respuestas: I shouldn't have told him the secret.
We shouldn't have told him the secret.
You shouldn't have told him the secret.
I should not have told him the secret.
He shouldn't have told him the secret.
She shouldn't have told him the secret.
They shouldn't have told him the secret.
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “shouldn't have done: something that was done and was not a good idea” applies. The original sentence, “It was a mistake to tell him the secret”, says that the secret was told and that it was a mistake. The transformation is shouldn't + have + told, the past participle of tell. As the original sentence has no personal subject, several subjects are accepted (I, we, you, she…).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Regret or criticism: shouldn't have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: No debería haberle contado el secreto.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I shouldn't have tell him the secret.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Tell is irregular and its past participle is told.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I shouldn't told him the secret.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Have is missing: modal + have + past participle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I mustn't have told him the secret.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Mustn't have does not express regret; to regret something you did, you use shouldn't have.

respuestas: They might have got lost
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “may / might / could have done: possibility about the past” applies. The order is subject (They), modal (might), have and the past participle. “Get lost” means to lose your way, and in the past it is built with the past participle got (or gotten in American English). The result is “They might have got lost”.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The expression is get lost: got goes before lost.
The modal goes before have: might have.
This is a question (“might they have got lost?”), not the statement that is required.

respuestas: You needn't have worried
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “needn't have done: it was done, but it wasn't necessary” applies. The person worried and it turned out to be unnecessary, which is exactly what needn't have expresses. The order is subject, needn't, have and the past participle worried. It is a typical sentence to reassure someone after something has turned out well.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: You worried unnecessarily: needn't have + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: No hacía falta que te preocuparas.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Needn't is the modal and goes before have: needn't have worried.
This is a question; the required sentence is a statement with the subject first.

descripcion_larga_es: Past modals (modal + have + past participle) let you deduce what happened (must have rained), rule it out (can't have finished), suggest possibilities (might have missed), criticise or regret (should have told) and imagine results (would have helped). They are essential at C1 level for reasoning about past events. Spanish speakers find them difficult because “debe de haber” and “debería haber” get mixed up, and Spanish does not distinguish needn't have done from didn't need to do.

contexto.que_es: It is the combination of a modal verb with have and the past participle to talk about actions before the present moment with a nuance of certainty, possibility, criticism or hypothesis. Each modal keeps its meaning: must for a confident deduction, can't for impossibility, might and could for possibility, should for criticism, would for a hypothetical result and needn't for something done unnecessarily.
contexto.por_que_importa: It lets you reason about the past without stating facts you don't know, something constant in analysis, debates and presentations. Confusing must have (deduction) with had to (obligation) or with mustn't (prohibition) completely changes the meaning. In a C1 exam the distinction between needn't have done and didn't need to do is particularly valued.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: It appears when there is evidence that leads to a conclusion (the lights are off), when regretting a decision (I shouldn't have eaten so much), when speculating about why someone hasn't arrived or when describing what would have happened in other circumstances. Spanish speakers tend to leave out have (you should told me) and to use must have for past obligation.
